title: How to work from a printed cross-stitch chart
subtitle: Using a paper chart to count, track progress, and maintain your place
excerpt: Working from a printed chart means counting stitches on paper and stitches on fabric at the same time, tracking which rows have been completed, and keeping your place through sessions and interruptions. Three habits make this manageable: marking off each completed row on the chart, using a magnetic board or ruler guide to hold the current row, and checking the count from a fixed reference point rather than from memory.
sourceNotes: Standard practice for working from printed cross-stitch charts. The magnetic board and ruler guide methods are widely documented.

content.text: Working from a printed chart is a reading-and-counting process that runs in parallel with the stitching. You look at the chart to know what to stitch, count the squares on the fabric to find the position, stitch the cross, and then mark your place on the chart before looking away. The mark-your-place step is the one that most beginners skip and then regret when they return to a piece after a day away.
Magnetic board and strips: a flat board with a strip of magnetic tape that holds a ruler across the chart. Move the strip down one row at a time. The ruler shows exactly which row is being worked.
Highlighter tape: removable highlighter tape placed along the current row. The tape is transparent, so the symbols remain readable underneath.

Pencil or erasable pen: mark a small dot on each stitched symbol as it is completed. Cross out each completed row at the end of a session. Erasable pen allows corrections if a row count needs revision.

Always count from a known fixed point, not from the previous stitch. The chart centre (marked with arrows) and the fabric centre are your primary reference. The gridded 10-by-10 blocks on the chart and the basting grid on the fabric are the secondary reference.
When you sit down after a break, do not continue from the last stitch. Count back from the nearest grid intersection on both the chart and the fabric to confirm you are in the right place.

If something looks off, count from two different directions to cross-check the position. A wrong count found early costs minutes to fix; a wrong count found twenty rows later can mean unpicking an entire section.

items.symptom: Position on the fabric does not match position on the chart after several sessions
items.cause: Progress was not marked on the chart at the end of each session, or counting resumed from the previous stitch rather than from a fixed reference.
items.fix: Mark every completed row before stopping. When resuming, always count from the nearest 10-by-10 grid intersection on both the chart and the fabric before stitching the first new cross.

content.text: For large projects where the chart is an A3 or larger printout, laminate the pages or protect them in a plastic sleeve. A chart that is handled every session will wear at the fold lines and the symbols will become hard to read.
